activities.caption: pair each classical device with its instance
activities.name: fomAncientMatch

config.prompt: The ancient grid in its actual machinery — pair each device with its instance:

pairs.left: juries filled by lottery rather than election
pairs.right: Athenians considered voting for officials aristocratic — the poor as fit to judge as the rich
exile a dangerous politician for ten years by write-in vote
the monarchic element of Rome's mixed constitution
the democratic element Polybius praised as self-balancing
not the structure but the aim

config.why: Rome's mixed constitution — consuls, senate, tribunes — was the arrangement the American founders studied directly.

activities.caption: bet the magnitude — Switzerland's referendum calendar
activities.name: fomSwissEstimate

config.prompt: How many national referendum days does Switzerland run each year?
config.why: Four a year, treated as routine — while most democracies treat referendums as fireworks: powerful, rare, and hard to unlight.
config.context: four national referendum days a year

activities.anchor: what does the representative owe the voter
activities.caption: file each feature under its institutional shape
activities.name: fomRegimeSort

config.prompt: Parliamentary versus presidential — file each feature:

items.label: the prime minister is chosen by, and sits in, parliament
a majority can remove a government in an afternoon (Callaghan, 1979)
the executive is elected separately for a fixed term

config.why: Both are democracies — they fail differently, and constitutions are largely bets about which failure mode you fear more.

config.text: The word 'liberal' means competitive elections %%0%% independent courts, a free press and enforceable rights that bind the winners too. Majorities without those restraints are %%1%%.
config.hint: One small connective and one long word for what unrestrained majorities become.

activities.anchor: outright dictatorships have become rarer than
activities.caption: one line of this autocratisation briefing is wrong
activities.name: fomAutoSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's briefing on modern autocracy is wrong — click it:
lines: Plain dictatorships are now less common than regimes that hold elections as theatre.
Electoral autocracies remove what elections are for: real opposition, real media, real courts.
The third wave of autocratisation proceeds mainly by military coups.
The erosion path: packing courts, capturing media, rewriting rules — each step individually defensible.
Iran's theocracy layers an elected president and parliament beneath an unelected Supreme Leader and clerical council.
config.correction: It is erosion, not coups — the regime slides election by election, out of the democratic column without a single tank in the street.
config.why: V-Dem now classifies most of the world's population as living under such regimes — the measurements count what happens around elections.

activities.caption: drag the divider — insider versus outsider tactics
activities.name: fomGroupsCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider — two routes for pressure groups:

before.label: insider route
before.text: Work through access: consultation, briefings, quiet amendments — influence exercised inside the room.

after.label: outsider route
after.text: Shut out of the room or refusing it: marches, boycotts, litigation, civil disobedience — Extinction Rebellion's strategy is explicitly this route.

config.why: Sectional groups (unions, business lobbies) and promotional groups (Amnesty, Greenpeace) both choose between the routes — and in most democracies, more detailed law is shaped in committee rooms than in chamber speeches.

activities.caption: file each right under its kind
activities.name: fomRightsSort

config.prompt: Negative versus positive rights — file each:

items.label: restrain the state — cost it restraint, not money
oblige provision — cost budgets, argued as policy as much as principle

config.why: Rights are not parchment but practices — they persist exactly as long as courts, presses and citizens keep enforcing them.

activities.anchor: redistributing the preferences of eliminated candidates
activities.caption: rebuild the ranked-choice count, step by step
activities.name: fomRcvOrder

config.prompt: How a ranked-choice count runs — assemble the sequence:
items: Voters order the candidates, first preference on top
The candidate at the bottom is eliminated
Their preferences are redistributed to the remaining candidates
The count repeats until one candidate commands a majority
config.why: No wasted-vote logic, and winners who can claim broader appeal — at the cost of a count most voters cannot replay in their heads.
